<reason>Both sides were disciplined, used proper A1:/A2: labelling, and stayed on the motion. A won because it identified and held the decisive pressure point — enforcement at both ends — and extracted two damaging concessions: that the only sanction is financial, and that there is no retention mechanism keeping relocated applicants in the assigned state. A's collapse argument ("your binding quota is my proposal wearing a court summons... the same relief, purchased twice: once in cash, once in cohesion") gave the judge a clean comparative reason to vote, and its correction that relocation occurs only after landing, screening and registration directly falsified B's "he never lands on Lesbos" line. B's best work was the honest ownership of the fine and the genuinely clarifying reframe that the real difference is where the default obligation sits — charity versus system — plus the sharp retort that "money alone never moves a single case off Lesbos" and the point that frontline states themselves demand redistribution. That kept B alive but did not neutralise the core problem: on B's own account, a tested quota yields euros from defectors and a mobile applicant in Frankfurt, which is close to A's model plus political cost. A also carried the backlash argument better; B's reply that resentment came from overload rather than distribution did not answer the concrete 2015 Visegrád example. A's two clipped turns are a real execution cost and narrow the margin, but the substance still favours A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure question demanding a named sanction and a named retention mechanism, and B's honest but concessive answer (financial fine; "I cannot promise the man stays in Latvia"), which A then converted into the "binding quota is my proposal wearing a court summons" collapse — reinforced by A's correction that relocation happens after landing and screening, gutting B's claim that the applicant never lands on Lesbos.</best_rebuttal>
